extracted.intended_audience: global patent counsel and patent practitioners advising on Canadian patentability/prior art
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether a reference or activity qualifies as prior art in Canada and for assessing novelty (anticipation) and inventive step (obviousness) of patent claims under Canadian law. Focuses on dates, public availability, claim construction, PSA, the Sanofi four-step obviousness test, enabling disclosure, and practical prosecution/validity considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art qualification under sections 28.2 and 28.3
rubrics_metrics.description: Canada places no blanket restriction on types of references or activities that can be prior art; instead sections 28.2 and 28.3 require the reference or activity to meet certain criteria (e.g., public availability before disclosure deadline) before it can be considered in an anticipation or obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the statutory criteria are met, the reference or activity can be considered prior art in an anticipation and/or obviousness analysis. The form or medium of disclosure (printed, digital, any language) is irrelevant so long as the subject-matter became available to the public in Canada or elsewhere. See also rules on disclosure deadlines, claim dates, and exceptions for applicant disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim date (section 28.1) and priority entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim date is the patent document's Canadian filing date or, where priority is validly claimed, the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To validly claim an earlier priority date: the subject matter must have been disclosed in an earlier patent document filed by the applicant or predecessor; the earlier filing must be in Canada or a treaty country; the earlier filing must be within 12 months; and a request for priority must be made. Claims in a later application can have different claim dates depending on whether they incorporate new material. PCT national phase filings can form the claim date basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure deadline rules (applicant vs non-applicant disclosures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure deadlines vary depending on who made the disclosure: disclosures by the applicant (or someone who obtained knowledge from the applicant) are only excluded if the application is filed within one year of that disclosure; disclosures by others must have been publicly available before the claimed invention's actual Canadian filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All potential prior art must be publicly available before either: one year before the effective filing date (if disclosed by applicant or someone who obtained knowledge from applicant) or the claimed invention's actual Canadian filing date (if not disclosed by applicant). For non-patent references, disclosure deadline is typically the publication date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-pending Canadian patent applications can be anticipatory
rubrics_metrics.description: A co-pending Canadian patent application (even if not yet published) can be anticipatory if that other patent document has a claim date that precedes the claim date of the subject claim in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under paragraph 28.2(1)(d), a pending application may invalidate a later claim where its claim date is earlier. Co-pending applications' claim dates are therefore relevant when determining anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public availability (objective test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference must be disclosed 'in such a manner that the subject-matter became available to the public in Canada or elsewhere' before its disclosure deadline; the test is objective — whether the public had the opportunity to access the reference, not whether anyone actually saw it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of publicly available references include published patents/applications, non-patent literature (including online postings), meetings, catalogs, and regulatory documents — provided members of the public are free at law and equity to use the information. Confidential disclosures, implicit duties of confidentiality, private manuscripts in non-accessible archives, etc., are not publicly available. Case law: Wenzel; Baker Petrolite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art activities as disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities (oral communications, prior use, prior sale, naturally occurring products) can constitute prior art provided they made the subject-matter available to the public before the disclosure deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public oral communications can be prior art if communicated to a member of the public free to use the information. Prior use/sale counts only to the extent it discloses the invention (enabling disclosure) and is not confidential or experimental in nature. Courts examine whether the public could glean information from the product (e.g., by reverse engineering without inventive skill). See Wenzel, Bayer, Bombardier examples and tests for experimental use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Public use of a product is not 'publicly available' if it can be proven the use was experimental in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To assess experimental use, courts look to whether the user believed the use was experimental (not the owner). Where use was experimental, the activity will not be considered in anticipation or obviousness inquiries. See Bayer Inc. v Apotex Inc., Bombardier, Conway, Martin v Ford Motor Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation test (Apotex v Sanofi): disclosure and enablement from a single reference/activity
rubrics_metrics.description: To be anticipatory, a single prior art reference or activity must both disclose the claimed subject matter and enable the claimed subject matter (the PSA may supply common general knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation requires a single reference or activity providing disclosure and enablement such that performing it would necessarily result in infringement of all essential claim elements. The test applies across technologies and types of patents. See Apotex v Sanofi; Aux Sable; Hoffmann‑La Roche v Sandoz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure requirement specifics (essential elements and inherent disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior art must disclose the essential elements of the claim; exact description is not required and inherent disclosure is possible where old/known subject matter is necessarily present in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A generic genus does not anticipate a later specific selection claim unless performing the generic necessarily infringes the specific claim. Conversely, a specific selection can anticipate a later general claim if performing the specific necessarily infringes the general. Case examples: Abbott, Shire, Swist v MEG Energy, Valence v Phostech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement for anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior art must be sufficiently detailed to enable a PSA to perform the claimed invention without the exercise of inventive ingenuity or undue experimentation (the PSA can rely on common general knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obvious errors/omissions that a skilled person could readily correct do not defeat enablement. Threshold for 'undue burden' depends on the field — in fields with routine trials the threshold is higher; routine trials generally are not undue, but prolonged/arduous experimentation is undue. See Apotex v Sanofi (para 37).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction: purposive & informed approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are construed in an informed and purposive manner as of the date the patent was published or laid open to public inspection; the PSA and common general knowledge are used to give words meaning and to distinguish essential from non-essential elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single construction is completed per claim and applied equally to infringement and validity. Claims should not be construed overly technically or literally, nor expanded by vague 'spirit' concepts. The specification and PSA common general knowledge inform construction, but extrinsic evidence like inventor notebooks and prior art are generally inadmissible except as allowed by statute (section 53.1(1)) or specific exceptions. Presumption that all elements are essential can be rebutted based on inventor's intentions and PSA understanding. See Free World Trust, Whirlpool, MOPOP s12.02.02e.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person skilled in the art (PSA) and common general knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The PSA is a notional person (or team) of ordinary competence, skill, and knowledge in the relevant field, reasonably diligent but unimaginative, and with a 'mind willing to understand' the specification; their common general knowledge informs claim construction, anticipation, and obviousness analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PSA is taken generously (not the most skilled nor the least qualified). Common general knowledge includes what PSAs generally know at the claim date and may include information passed informally (discussions), attitudes, trends, expectations, and sometimes patents, but not all public-domain information. The field's technical complexity affects PSA definition (e.g., 'rocket science patents'). See Janssen-Ortho, Whirlpool, Apotex v Sanofi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness/sanity check: Sanofi four-step test
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness is assessed claim-by-claim using the Sanofi four-step test: (1) identify the PSA and common general knowledge; (2) identify the inventive concept (or construe it); (3) identify differences between the state of the art and the inventive concept; (4) decide whether those differences would have been obvious to the PSA (inventive step).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Sanofi test is the canonical framework in Canada (derived from UK Windsurfing/Pozzoli jurisprudence). There is no 'prima facie' concept in Canada; multiple prior art pieces can form a 'mosaic' for the state of the art, including foreign-language and non-analogous references, but courts must still consider whether the PSA would have combined them. See Apotex v Sanofi and related case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of the inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the inventive concept of the claim (the 'solution taught by the patent'); if not readily apparent, construe it using the claims and, if necessary, the specification, taking care not to improperly narrow or expand the claim by reading the spec.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construing the inventive concept is distinct from but related to claim construction. Using the specification is allowed when the inventive concept isn't apparent from the claims, especially for chemical/bare-formula claims, but avoid imputing optional dependent claim limitations into independent claims. One inventive concept may flow through all claims; overlap is expected. See Shire, Mylan, Tetra Tech examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between inventive concept and the state of the art (mosaic and combination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the inventive concept to the 'mosaic' of prior art (which may include multiple references across languages and fields) to identify differences and consider whether a PSA would have thought to combine those pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the mosaic contains all aspects of the inventive concept, the fourth Sanofi stage still requires analysis of whether combination would have been obvious. Consider obscurity/difficulty of finding pieces and whether they lie outside the field (reducing likelihood of combination). Case examples: Hospira, Allergan v Apotex, Google v Sonos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventiveness determination (stage four) and anti‑hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether differences between the state of the art and the inventive concept would have been obvious to the PSA without knowledge of the invention, avoiding hindsight bias; inventive ingenuity can lie in idea conception, putting it into practice, or in combining known parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider factual/contextual factors including climate in the field, motivation to solve the problem, time/effort to create the invention, likelihood and motivation to combine disclosures, and whether other pathways pointed away. Use MOPOP guidance and case law (Bridgeview, Janssen‑Ortho, Tensar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious-to-try considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: For fields where advances are often won by experimentation, courts may apply an 'obvious to try' test considering whether it was more or less self-evident to try to obtain the claimed invention and whether there were a finite number of predictable solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors: whether it was self-evident that the approach ought to work; whether finite predictable solutions existed; the extent and nature of effort required (routine vs prolonged/arduous); and whether prior art provided motivation. The inventor's history (how the invention was reached) may also be relevant. See Apotex v Sanofi, Hospira guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (objective indicia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts and examiners may consider secondary (contextual) factors as instructive in the obviousness inquiry, including commercial success, industry conduct/failed attempts, long-felt need, conventional wisdom, and imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations are not determinative by themselves but can be persuasive. Evidence must be tied to the inventive concept (commercial success attributable to claimed invention). Examples of admissible evidence: financial/sales data, awards, competitor actions. Be cautious filing commercially sensitive evidence in prosecution because Canadian Patent Office cannot impose confidentiality orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and admissibility limits for claim construction and prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally extrinsic evidence (inventor notebooks, prior art, contemporary documents) is not admissible for claim construction, except statutory exceptions such as section 53.1(1) communications with the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 53.1(1) allows written communications between applicant and the Canadian Patent Office to be admitted to rebut representations about claim construction. Otherwise, rely on claims, specification, and PSA common general knowledge for construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical prosecution and validity considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical recommendations for searching, prosecution, responding to examiner objections, and court pleadings: use commercial search tools, search competitor portfolios, place watches, challenge examiners who fail to apply the Sanofi test properly, consider claim amendments, and plead all prior art when litigating (no opposition procedure in Canada).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial search tools yield broader results than free tools. When challenging examiner obviousness objections, applicants can argue failure to properly apply the four-step Sanofi test and may amend claims. In court, pleadings must expressly include all prior art intended to be relied upon; new prior art requires amended pleadings. Note Canada lacks an opposition procedure; validity is challenged in courts.
